If a person enters a grove of campaka trees, they do not smell any other fragrance; who, then, would take pleasure in the merits of the Two Vehicles?
That one need not bow to their seat and that flowers do not cling to their body—all such persons are of the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
Thus, people are thereby prolonged.
Because form is boundless, prajñā is also boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, prajñā is also boundless.
This, then, is where the principle prevails.
One should know that in the former teaching, the doctrine, the practice, the person, and the principle were all superior; being superior, it was sublime.

If you claim that the present [teaching] is superior in its functional application, why then do you say that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a teaching of concealed intent, and thus its doctrine is inferior?
When the characteristics of concealment are practiced, the practice is deficient;
when the characteristics of concealment do not clarify the Buddha-nature, the principle is deficient.
Since both the "Four" and the "One" are lacking, what is now practiced is both deficient and coarse.
Since their duration in the past was already long, being long implies they were sublime.

Regarding the four difficulties concerning the breadth and narrowness of the essence of the fruit: if the essence of the fruit in the past were incomplete in its manifold virtues—whether as having remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*)—and were thus narrow or coarse, how could this possibly be so?
Prajñā is the Mother of Buddhas, and all Buddhas of the ten directions protect it.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"I have never before heard this profound sūtra of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). One should know that the essence of the former fruit is fully endowed with all virtues.

If it is claimed that the essence of the present fruit is vast and should therefore be complete and fully realized, why then do you further say that it is both complete and incomplete, and both realized and unrealized?
Why do you further say that the fruit of Buddhahood is impermanent, and likewise lacks self, bliss, and purity?
If all virtues were lacking, where would the "extensive meaning" lie?
If the essence is extensive, the Dharma-body should pervade all places; why, then, is it further said that his lifespan ended at eighty?
Or, having entered cessation through the severance of ashes for seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, does one depart from here without reaching there?
If you say its substance is vast, then one should be able to see the Buddha-nature with all five eyes.
One should know that the present fruition lacks four of the "four ones," and is thus narrow yet coarse;
when compared to the past, the past remains superior.

Regarding the four difficulties concerning the high and low levels of the fruition stage: if the present fruition stage were high, how could its established teaching be placed below the fifth teaching?
Why does practice not transcend impermanence?
Why does the person not transcend transformation?
Why does principle not exhaust the secret treasury?
One should know that the present stage of fruition lacks four of the "four ones," as it is entirely inferior and coarse;
whereas the former stage of fruition possessed all four, being entirely sublime and wondrous.
Regarding the difficulty concerning the long or short duration of the fruit's function: if the function of the present fruit were long-lasting, why would the teaching not clarify its permanence?
Why do practices not suddenly shatter ignorance?
Why is a person not immediately Vairocana?
Why is principle not immediately the secret treasury?
One should know that in the present fruit there is no sublime Dharma; is this not, then, coarse?
And yet you further speak of "extending life through supernormal powers"—what kind of supernormal power is this?
If it is a supernormal power produced through mental effort (*manasikāra*), it is the same as those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If it is untainted supernatural power (*anāsrava-abhijñā*), it is the same as that of the Lesser Vehicle;
if it is supernatural power of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-abhijñā*), then it neither prolongs nor does not prolong, yet it is able to prolong and able not to prolong.
If you can extend [life], why stop at extending it? Why not extend the eyes so they may see the Buddha-nature?
Why not extend the tongue so it may preach of the eternal?
If the eyes do not see this nature, then know that these are not the supernatural powers of the true mark (*dharmatā*). If they are not coarse, what are they called?
The former objection has already been understood as coarse; the latter objection merely recurs again.
That [text] uses six types of cause and effect to distinguish the coarse from the subtle, and further employs the four "ones" exclusively to judge what is subtle.
If one challenges the "coarse" [teachings] by asserting that they all possess the fourfold unity, then the former "coarse" is not truly coarse;
if one challenges the "sublime" [teachings] by asserting that they entirely lack the fourfold unity, then the present "sublime" is not truly sublime.
Regarding each single phrase, if one were to apply these fourfold challenges, there would be twenty-four such points (four for each of the six phrases).
Because they employ those contradictions to strike at their own characteristics, they neither increase nor decrease; it should be understood as merely this much.
